name: Benchmark employer brand on Glassdoor with Bright Data, OpenAI and Slack

parameters.content:
## Benchmark your employer brand against the companies you lose people to

Put your Glassdoor reviews URL and a few competitors' in `Settings`. This scores all of them on the seven dimensions Glassdoor breaks out and tells you which one you are actually behind on.

### How it works

`days` does not limit how much you get: 90 and 365 both return exactly 100 reviews, so a busy employer's hundred covers two months and a quiet one's covers two years.

`Line Up The Windows` fixes that. It finds the shortest span in the set and cuts every company back to it, then prints the window and how many reviews each company has left inside it.

Each company is crawled on its own pass of the loop: a snapshot caps at 100 rows across every input it holds, so one crawl asking for three returns one company's hundred and nothing at all for the rest.

Every run stores its scores, so the next says which way each company moved.

Each dimension is averaged over the reviews that answered it. The six sub-ratings are only about 73% filled, so dividing by the row count would understate every score by roughly a quarter and look like a finding.

Current and former employees are counted separately, matched by prefix because `employee_type` is free text with eleven variants.

### Setup

Add a **Header Auth** credential called `Authorization` with the value `Bearer YOUR_BRIGHT_DATA_KEY`.

Create a Data Table called `employer_brand` with a text column for each of `employer_id`, `company`, `is_you`, `checked_on`, `window_from`, `window_to`, `reviews_in_window`, `overall`, `pay`, `culture`, `work_life`, `leadership`, `career`, `diversity` and `would_recommend_pct`.

In `Settings`, paste the Glassdoor reviews URLs. They look like `glassdoor.com/Reviews/Atlassian-Reviews-E115699.htm` - the number after the E is the employer id and a wrong one costs ten minutes before it fails. Point Slack wherever you want it.

## 1. You and the companies you lose people to
The employer id is the number after the E in the URL. A wrong one costs ten minutes before it fails.

## 2. One company per pass
A snapshot caps at 100 rows across every input it holds, and the first company to finish takes the lot. Sent one at a time, each gets its own hundred.

## 3. Wait it out, then take what came back
A company that returns nothing still has to re-enter the loop. A branch that ends in zero items does not, and the run would stop there with nothing red.

## 4. The same dates for everybody
One hundred reviews come back whatever the day count says, so each company's hundred covers a different span. Everyone is cut to the shortest.

## 5. Read the dimension you lose on
The cons arrive as their own field, so the model is never asked to split a review into good and bad.

## 6. A score per company, and which way it moved
The table keeps one row per employer id, so the next run can say what changed rather than printing the same number again.

## 7. When it breaks
An Error Trigger is a separate entry point, so a failed run says so in Slack instead of going quiet.

## One hundred reviews, whatever you ask for

`days: 90` and `days: 365` both return 100. It is a hard cap, newest first, so the window each company covers depends on how often it is reviewed. Nothing below compares two companies until both have been cut to the same dates.

=Below are the "cons" fields from recent Glassdoor reviews of one company, written by its own current and former employees. The company scores worse than its competitors on {{ $json.worst_label }}.

{{ $json.cons_brief }}

Write two or three sentences saying what these complaints have in common, in plain language, for the person who has to do something about it. Quote at most one short phrase. Do not repeat the score, do not give advice, and do not soften it.
If the complaints have nothing in common, say that instead and name the two or three separate things they are about.
